evidence.claim: Reuters reported that AMLO said his government would channel a quarter of its publicity budget into health insurance and pensions for poorer journalists, while noting the move could affect traditional media revenues and reflected a fractious relationship with critical outlets.

evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy and rhetoric on the media environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO as a government action; the press-effect analysis is interpretive but tied to his announcement.
contrary_evidence: This could be read as welfare support for precarious journalists rather than pure coercion.
The article itself notes a possible revenue hit to traditional media, so the measure is mixed rather than clearly protective.

evidence.title: Ejecutivo Federal abusa del poder público para estigmatizar a la prensa
evidence.claim: ARTICLE 19 condemned AMLO's morning conference attack on Carlos Loret de Mola, saying the president denigrated and criminalized the journalist by exposing alleged income data in a way that was intimidating and violated press freedom and privacy standards.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct contemporaneous rights-organization statement describing a specific ruler-attributed press incident.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 incident in the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO because the complaint concerns his own public conference and remarks.
contrary_evidence: The government could argue it was criticizing alleged false reporting rather than suppressing journalism.
The article is advocacy-oriented, so the precise legal characterization is stronger than the normative conclusion.

evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Mexico
evidence.claim: The report says independent media often self-censored due to fear of reprisals, that politicians including President López Obrador publicly discredited journalists as biased or corrupt, and that the 'Who's Who in Lies' segment worsened official discrediting of press workers.
evidence.locator: lines 139-140 and 237-239, plus executive summary context
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Annual government human-rights report with direct factual descriptions of the 2022 press environment and state treatment of journalists.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on 2022; strong because it directly reports the target year's conditions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: AMLO-specific in the sense that the report names him as a discrediting actor and ties the media segment to his morning conference; other pressures are broader context.
contrary_evidence: The report also says the government generally respected free expression and that independent media remained active.
Some intimidation came from criminal groups, not only the president or his administration.

evidence.title: New Pegasus Spyware Abuses Identified in Mexico
evidence.publisher: The Citizen Lab, University of Toronto
evidence.claim: Citizen Lab and R3D found Pegasus infections against Mexican journalists and a human rights defender between 2019 and 2021, after Mexico's current president had assured the public that the government no longer used the spyware and that there would be no further abuses.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Technical forensic work from a respected research lab, with clear victim identification and temporal attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Published in 2022 and directly relevant to the ruler's 2022 position on surveillance, though the infections themselves span 2019-2021.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable at least to the current administration's denial and failure to stop the abuse; the report does not by itself name every operator or issue a full command chain.
contrary_evidence: The infections are partly retrospective to 2019-2021, so they are best used as evidence of continuing abuse under the administration rather than a new 2022 incident.
The report does not by itself prove that AMLO personally ordered each infection.

reasons.reason: This Pegasus evidence is partly retrospective to 2019-2021; it should be used as continuing-surveillance context, not as a new 2022 incident.

evidence.title: Mexico: Army used Pegasus spyware against journalists and activists
evidence.claim: ARTICLE 19 said the Army Spies investigation provided clear evidence that illegal Pegasus surveillance continued under the current administration and that the targeted victims included journalists and a human rights defender investigating military abuses.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Strong rights-organization synthesis of a forensic investigation, though it remains a secondary interpretation of technical findings.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 surveillance and press-freedom concerns, even though the infections themselves began earlier.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the current administration and the military apparatus under AMLO, but the report stops short of proving his personal operational order.
contrary_evidence: The government denied the allegations and disputed the attribution.
The article is advocacy-oriented, so the operational conclusion should be triangulated with the technical report.

reasons.reason: This is a secondary advocacy synthesis of a forensic investigation; it is useful, but should not be treated as a stand-alone finding on command responsibility.

evidence.title: The right to protest is under threat in Mexico
evidence.claim: Amnesty said police violently and disproportionately repressed a peaceful student protest, used racist, classist and misogynistic insults, detained 93 people, and that the abuses remained unpunished a year later, illustrating a continuing threat to protest rights in Mexico.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Detailed contemporaneous rights reporting with named incident, victims, and remedy failure, though the core incident occurred in 2021.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective 2021 incident published in 2022; useful for the 2022 pattern and aftermath, not a fresh 2022 crackdown order.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The episode is attributed to state police under the national political environment; direct federal command is weaker than for the presidential press or electoral reforms.
contrary_evidence: The incident predates the publication year, so it is better evidence of 2022 aftermath and pattern than of a new 2022 decision.
The article focuses on one state-level episode, not a full nationwide repression system.

evidence.title: Mexico: 2022 Article IV Consultation-Press Release and Staff Report
evidence.claim: Mexico’s recovery was gradual, inflation became entrenched, and the government maintained a broadly neutral fiscal stance in 2022 while using largely untargeted subsidies to mitigate the rise in the cost of living.
evidence.locator: press release summary / opening summary paragraph
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary IMF country surveillance with direct macro-fiscal assessment and a precise 2022 time fit.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 target-period macro and fiscal conditions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to the AMLO government because the fiscal stance and subsidy choices were government policy, but the inflation shock also reflected global conditions.
contrary_evidence: The IMF frames much of the pressure as a pandemic and global inflation shock, not purely a ruler-made problem.
The same source does not by itself prove distributional effectiveness or broad-based gains.

reasons.reason: This is macro context on inflation and fiscal stance; it should not be read as direct proof of AMLO's competence without the other policy evidence.

evidence.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022
evidence.claim: Mexico’s solid macroeconomic policy framework safeguarded stability, but long-run growth was low and productivity was hindered by informality, financial exclusion, corruption, weak investment, and low female labor-force participation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative independent country survey from the OECD; broad but directly relevant structural diagnosis.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year-adjacent baseline and inherited-constraint context for 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited and structural, though the policy environment under AMLO mattered for investment and competition.
contrary_evidence: The OECD also says the macro policy framework remained solid, so the case is mixed rather than uniformly negative.
Low growth alone does not prove ruler culpability.

evidence.title: Key Policy Insights: OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022
evidence.claim: Investment was weak and domestic policy uncertainty increased, especially after proposals to reform the electricity market; the OECD urged certainty about existing contracts and regulatory stability.
evidence.locator: section on restarting investment and boosting productivity
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent policy analysis with explicit causation and clear relevance to ruler-period policy choices.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 policy settings and investor expectations.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly relevant to AMLO because the uncertainty arose from his government’s energy-policy proposals and regulatory direction.
contrary_evidence: The OECD also says Mexico could benefit from U.S. recovery and nearshoring, so the environment was not uniformly adverse.
Investment weakness predates 2022, so this is partly inherited.

evidence.title: Key Policy Insights: OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022
evidence.claim: Support to PEMEX had increased to about 1 percent of GDP and PEMEX remained a significant risk for the sovereign.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent expert assessment with a concrete fiscal magnitude and risk statement.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to AMLO’s energy strategy and repeated support for state oil and power firms, though the fiscal risk is also structural.
contrary_evidence: Energy security and state-capacity arguments can explain some support to PEMEX.
The OECD note is a policy warning, not proof that the spending was wholly wasteful.

evidence.title: Mexico, Colombia enact big rate hikes amid stubborn inflation
evidence.claim: The Bank of Mexico raised its benchmark interest rate 75 basis points to a record 9.25 percent as inflation remained above target and persistent.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a concrete central-bank decision with clear numerical detail and date fit.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 macro context, though monetary policy was not under AMLO’s direct control.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Only indirect attribution because Banxico is independent; this is mainly context for the economic environment AMLO governed in.
contrary_evidence: This does not show an AMLO policy choice because the central bank is independent.
It mainly constrains credit and growth rather than proving any ruler failure.

reasons.reason: Banxico is independent, so this is primarily macro context rather than a ruler-attributed policy action.

evidence.title: Mexico anti-inflation subsidies come with $28 billion price tag
evidence.claim: Mexico’s anti-inflation subsidies cost about 575 billion pesos in 2022, including 430 billion pesos for gasoline subsidies, 73 billion for domestic energy subsidies, and 69 billion for food-security measures.
evidence.locator: Reuters story text / government figures cited in article
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters cites government figures and provides clear policy composition and fiscal scale.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy response to inflation during the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to the AMLO government because officials announced and defended the measures alongside the president.
contrary_evidence: The measures were large and partly untargeted, so they may have been blunt rather than efficient.
The fiscal cost was high even if the policy eased consumer pain.

evidence.title: Entra en vigor incremento al salario mínimo del 22%
evidence.publisher: Secretaría del Trabajo y Previsión Social
evidence.claim: The 2022 minimum wage increase was 22 percent, the largest in 34 years, and it was said to benefit about 6 million workers directly.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary government labor announcement with a concrete policy change and target population.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy choice in the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO’s administration because it was the government’s wage policy and was announced in the president’s orbit.
contrary_evidence: Higher minimum wages can add inflation pressure, so the policy has tradeoffs.
The press release is promotional and does not by itself prove full distributional success.

evidence.title: El impacto del salario minimo en la pobreza
evidence.publisher: Comisión Nacional de los Salarios Mínimos
evidence.claim: The study estimates a negative elasticity of the minimum wage on poverty and says that 4.1 million of the 5.1 million people who left poverty between 2018 and 2022 can be attributed exclusively to minimum-wage increases.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official analytical study with a concrete estimate, but it is retrospective and not fully independent of the policy agenda.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on 2018-2022, so it fits the target period as an after-the-fact estimate rather than contemporaneous evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to AMLO because the wage path was a core policy of his administration, but the estimate is retrospective and not solely his doing.
contrary_evidence: The estimate is model-based and retrospective, not a contemporaneous census of causation.
The study does not isolate the minimum wage from other contributors such as remittances or the labor market.

evidence.title: Comunicado No. 47 Financiamiento para el impulso al nearshoring, con énfasis en la región del sur-sureste de México
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público
evidence.claim: The finance ministry announced a 200 million dollar BID credit line to support nearshoring and said Mexico could gain 35 billion dollars, equivalent to 2.6 percent of GDP, especially in the south-southeast.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary policy announcement with concrete financing and projected gains, though the gain estimate is forward-looking.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy action and target-year industrial strategy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO’s government because it was a federal financing plan announced by Hacienda under his administration.
contrary_evidence: The projected gain is an estimate, not a realized outcome.
Nearshoring potential also depends on external demand and private investment, not only on AMLO.

evidence.title: PEF 2022 garantiza continuidad de programas sociales y obras de desarrollo
evidence.publisher: Presidencia de la República 2018-2024 | Gobierno | gob.mx
evidence.claim: The 2022 federal budget was presented as guaranteeing continuity for welfare programs, pensions, scholarships, producer support, and strategic infrastructure works such as Tren Maya, Dos Bocas, and the AIFA.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary budget-policy statement from the presidency with concrete spending priorities.
evidence.period_fit: Budget for the target year, announced shortly before 2022 began.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO because this was the executive budget priority he promoted.
contrary_evidence: Announcements do not prove implementation quality or economic payoff.
Strategic megaprojects may have large opportunity costs or weak returns.

evidence.title: 12.10.22 Versión estenográfica de la conferencia de prensa matutina del presidente Andrés Manuel López Obrador
evidence.publisher: Presidencia de la República 2018-2024 | Gobierno | gob.mx
evidence.claim: AMLO described direct school budgets, scholarships, pensions for older adults, disability support, and a planned 25 percent pension increase, all as part of his administration’s welfare system.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary ruler speech documenting policy priorities and implementation details.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 ruler-period policy speech and program description.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Fully attributable to AMLO as his own official morning conference and stated policy agenda.
contrary_evidence: This is implementation rhetoric, not independent proof of final welfare outcomes.
The benefits may be offset by inflation and other macro pressures.

evidence.title: EL CONEVAL PRESENTA INFORMACIÓN REFERENTE A LA POBREZA LABORAL AL CUARTO TRIMESTRE DE 2022
evidence.claim: Between the fourth quarter of 2021 and the fourth quarter of 2022, labor poverty fell from 40.3 percent to 38.5 percent, real labor income per capita rose 4.3 percent, and the number of employed people increased by 1.7 million, though labor poverty remained above pre-pandemic levels.
evidence.locator: bullet summary and discussion around lines 153-180
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary national statistics source with precise 2022 household-labor measures.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the target year and closes the year with official 2022 labor-market evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to AMLO only in the sense that his wage and welfare policies were one input; the report itself also reflects external recovery and labor-market dynamics.
contrary_evidence: The report does not isolate AMLO policy from the broader recovery.
Labor poverty was still above pre-pandemic levels.

evidence.title: Comunicado No. 7, El CONEVAL presenta las estimaciones de pobreza multidimensional 2022
evidence.claim: Between 2018 and 2022, multidimensional poverty in Mexico fell from 41.9 percent to 36.3 percent, and the number of people in poverty fell from 51.9 million to 46.8 million.
evidence.locator: page 0 and page 3 of the PDF, lines 13-19 and 136-147
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary official poverty release with explicit national estimates and a clear target-year fit.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on the 2018-2022 period, directly covering the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to AMLO because it captures his full sexenio to 2022, but the report itself also reflects pandemic recovery and remittances.
contrary_evidence: The period starts in 2018, so part of the change predates some 2022 policy choices.
The report does not itself isolate the contribution of one president versus external conditions.

evidence.title: Remittances to Mexico again break record on back of strong U.S. labor market
evidence.claim: Remittances to Mexico reached a record high in July 2022 at 5.3 billion dollars, and Reuters attributed part of the surge to the strong U.S. labor market.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting gives a concrete external condition that materially affected Mexican household income in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly external rather than AMLO-attributable; useful as a counterweight against over-crediting domestic policy for household gains.
contrary_evidence: The growth came largely from conditions in the United States, not Mexican policy.
High inflation meant remittances did not translate one-for-one into better real purchasing power.

reasons.reason: This is an external remittance driver, useful as a counterweight, but not AMLO-driven performance evidence.

evidence.title: Mexican president's contentious electricity overhaul defeated in Congress
evidence.claim: AMLO’s plan to increase state control of electricity generation was defeated in Congress, with opponents warning it would hurt investment and breach international obligations.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a concrete legislative defeat with direct policy implications for investment and competition.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy conflict in the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable because it was AMLO’s plan and his governing coalition pushed it.
contrary_evidence: AMLO framed the overhaul as protecting public interest and energy sovereignty.
Congress defeated the constitutional version, so the final policy outcome was partly blocked rather than fully enacted.

evidence.title: PEF 2022 garantiza continuidad de programas sociales y obras de desarrollo
evidence.claim: AMLO said the 2022 federal budget would provide sufficient resources for social programs and guaranteed continuity for adult pensions, disability benefits, student scholarships, producer support, and strategic development works.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary presidential budget statement; precise on priorities but self-reported.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO as president and budget agenda setter, though execution depended on ministries and later implementation.
contrary_evidence: Budget intent does not by itself prove delivery quality, coverage, or equity.

evidence.title: Programas para el Bienestar llegan a 25 millones de hogares; presupuesto prioriza a adultos mayores e indígenas, afirma presidente
evidence.claim: AMLO said federal wellbeing programs reached 25 million households and that adults mayores and indigenous people were among the most benefited groups.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential statement with concrete coverage figures, though still a self-report.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct federal policy claim by AMLO; beneficiary reach still depends on implementation by agencies and local delivery systems.
contrary_evidence: Household reach alone does not prove service quality or absence of exclusion.

evidence.title: DECRETO por el que se crea el organismo público descentralizado denominado Servicios de Salud del IMSS para el Bienestar (IMSS-BIENESTAR)
evidence.claim: The decree created IMSS-BIENESTAR and states its purpose as the progressive, quantitative, and qualitative extension of free health services for people who do not have social security.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official legal instrument with direct normative effect and explicit purpose language.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO because he signed the decree as president; later rollout and federalization involved other institutions.
contrary_evidence: The decree sets up the institution, but 2022 by itself does not prove nationwide service quality or completion.

evidence.title: Servicios de salud IMSS-BIENESTAR
evidence.claim: IMSS-BIENESTAR says it was born on 31 August 2022 to guarantee free medical care and medicines for people without social security.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official implementing-agency description of the new health institution and its mandate.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year founding and early rollout context.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the AMLO administration and federal health restructuring, but current website language reflects later institutional consolidation.
contrary_evidence: The page also reflects later expansion and retrospective institutional framing.

evidence.title: Realiza Secretaría de Bienestar pagos de pensiones y apoyos del primer bimestre del año a 10.4 millones de derechohabientes
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Bienestar / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: In the first bimestre of 2022, the government dispersed pension and welfare payments to 10.4 million rightsholders, including 9.2 million adult pension beneficiaries and 927,742 disability pension beneficiaries.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary government release with specific beneficiary counts and payment amounts.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct federal program delivery under AMLO; the release reflects executive policy but not independent auditing of results.
contrary_evidence: The figures measure coverage and disbursement, not program adequacy or impact.

evidence.title: Secretaría de Bienestar dispersa 46.7 mil mdp a 12.1 millones de derechohabientes de pensiones y programas
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Bienestar / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: The government said 12.1 million beneficiaries received September-October 2022 pension and welfare payments and that these transfers were made directly, without intermediaries.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary administrative release with concrete beneficiary and disbursement totals.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to AMLO-era federal welfare administration, though direct delivery is executed by agencies and Banco del Bienestar.
contrary_evidence: Direct delivery does not by itself exclude local-level patronage or uneven take-up.

evidence.title: Pensión para el Bienestar de las Personas con Discapacidad Permanente
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Bienestar / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: The program page says the disability pension seeks to improve income for people with permanent disability and explicitly frames the program as a rights-based tool for children, adolescents, youth, indigenous people, and Afro-Mexicans facing disability, discrimination, and racism.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official program design page with explicit target groups and purpose statement.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year policy design and implementation context.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct federal program design under AMLO; target-group emphasis is attributable, though actual uptake varies by state and registration stage.
contrary_evidence: The page is program design, not an independent outcome evaluation.

evidence.title: 1.3 millones de personas ya reciben Pensión para el Bienestar de las Personas con Discapacidad, con inversión de 22 mil mdp
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Bienestar / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: By December 2022, the disability pension served 1,301,922 people with 22 billion pesos in social investment, and the government described the program as being universal in 14 entities.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary government release with explicit beneficiary and funding figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the AMLO administration and intergovernmental agreements, though universalization was shared with state governments.
contrary_evidence: Universalization was incomplete nationwide, so this was expansion rather than full national coverage.

evidence.title: Entrega SEP más de 44 mil millones de pesos en becas Benito Juárez durante el primer semestre de 2022: CNBBBJ
evidence.publisher: Coordinación Nacional de Becas para el Bienestar Benito Juárez / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: In the first half of 2022, Mexico delivered more than 44 billion pesos in Benito Juárez scholarships to over 10 million students, with priority placement in indigenous and very high-margin schools to reduce dropout.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary education-program release with concrete funding, beneficiary, and targeting figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the federal executive and education bureaucracy; local school conditions still mediate delivery.
contrary_evidence: Coverage figures do not by themselves establish learning quality or completion outcomes.

evidence.title: Entrega Producción para el Bienestar apoyos directos para más de 1.7 millones de productores de pequeña y mediana escala
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: By March 2022, Producción para el Bienestar had transferred 12.5 billion pesos to support 1,766,430 small- and medium-scale producers through direct payments intended to provide liquidity for inputs and labor and strengthen food supply for families and communities.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary agriculture ministry release with precise beneficiary and transfer figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct federal agricultural policy under AMLO; it supports rural producers, though broader market conditions also affect farm incomes.
contrary_evidence: The release is self-reported and does not independently verify end-user welfare effects.

evidence.title: Entra en vigor incremento al salario mínimo del 22%
evidence.publisher: Secretaría del Trabajo y Previsión Social / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: The 2022 minimum wage increase was 22 percent, the largest in 34 years, and the government said it directly benefited 6 million workers while recovering 71 percent of the minimum wage's purchasing power.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary labor-policy announcement with specific wage and beneficiary figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to the AMLO administration through the federal wage-setting process, though the tripartite wage commission shares formal authority.
contrary_evidence: The statement is policy intent and summary, not an independent estimate of full distributional effects.

evidence.title: Incremento de los salarios mínimos impulsa crecimiento del ingreso laboral y reducción de la pobreza laboral
evidence.publisher: Comisión Nacional de los Salarios Mínimos / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: The CONASAMI analysis said that of the 5.1 million people who left poverty between 2018 and 2022, 4.1 million could be attributed exclusively to minimum-wage increases.
evidence.locator: analysis summary in press release body
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Government technical estimate with a direct causal claim, but it is a retrospective commission analysis rather than an external independent audit.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective analysis of the 2018-2022 period with a 2022 endpoint.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to AMLO's wage policy; the estimate is model-based and does not isolate every other macro or labor-market driver.
contrary_evidence: Causal attribution comes from the wage commission itself and should be treated cautiously as a government estimate.

reasons.reason: This is a retrospective government estimate of minimum-wage effects; it is useful context, not contemporaneous proof of 2022 welfare impact.

evidence.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022
evidence.claim: The OECD said Mexico's poverty and regional inequalities remain high, medium-term growth has weakened, weak investment and low female participation persist, and social spending and public investment have increased while health and education systems remain strained and infrastructure gaps remain significant.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent multilateral survey with explicit 2022 assessment and detailed policy diagnostics.
evidence.period_fit: Directly about the target year environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Only partly attributable to AMLO because the report also emphasizes pandemic, structural, and long-run constraints.
contrary_evidence: The same survey says Mexico has a solid macroeconomic framework, so the picture is mixed rather than uniformly negative.

evidence.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022 - Key Policy Insights
evidence.claim: The OECD noted that only 57 percent of federal social programmes had a beneficiary registry and recommended reducing fragmentation and duplication to extend coverage, especially for low-income households.
evidence.locator: key policy insights / social protection section
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Specific structural finding from a major multilateral survey, directly tied to social-program administration.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Relevant to federal social-policy capacity under AMLO, but not a direct finding of personal intent or misconduct.
contrary_evidence: The survey also notes that the number of social-program recipients had recently increased.

evidence.title: Informe de Evaluación de la Política de Desarrollo Social 2022
evidence.claim: CONEVAL's 2022 development-social-policy evaluation covers 2018-2022, diagnoses distributive-incidence and course-of-life gaps, and says there are growing inequalities affecting groups such as the indigenous population and a lack of integrated vision in parts of the social-policy portfolio.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Domestic evaluation body with a formal statutory mandate and explicit 2018-2022 coverage.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective but explicitly centered on the target period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but material: it evaluates the federal social-policy environment under AMLO rather than a single program.
contrary_evidence: The same report also notes advances in the incorporation of rights and course-of-life approaches.

evidence.title: Informe Anual 2022 | UNICEF México
evidence.claim: UNICEF reported significant advances in 2022 across health and nutrition, education, child protection, and social protection, including support to the Mexican government in designing and expanding priority social-protection programs and in recovering learning after COVID-19.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent UN agency report summarizing implemented work with government counterparts in the target year.
evidence.period_fit: Directly about 2022 with a 2023 publication date.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to AMLO-era federal policy because UNICEF describes support to the Mexican government, but it is not a unilateral government audit.
contrary_evidence: UNICEF also emphasizes remaining gaps and the need for continued public investment.

evidence.title: Teaching at the Right Level supports learning recovery in Mexico
evidence.claim: UNICEF says Mexico's Ministry of Education, with UNICEF and partners, ran government-led learning camps that reached thousands of children with targeted literacy and numeracy instruction and produced measurable gains in weeks.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct program case study with explicit intervention design and short-term outcome language.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the education ministry under the AMLO administration, though UNICEF and partners co-implemented the intervention.
contrary_evidence: The case study itself says Mexico's education system had long faced deep inequities and severe pre-COVID foundational-skill gaps.

evidence.title: Salud y nutrición infantil en México
evidence.claim: UNICEF says Mexican children and adolescents face a triple burden of malnutrition alongside inequitable access to primary care, vaccination, and WASH, and that it supports the government with a first-1,000-days program using supplementation, breastfeeding support, vaccination, neonatal screening, and early stimulation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent UN agency page with a detailed description of needs and current technical support to the government.
evidence.period_fit: Current explanatory page describing ongoing 2022-relevant conditions and interventions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Relevant to AMLO-era public-health and nutrition policy, but it is primarily an institutional support description rather than a presidential act record.
contrary_evidence: The page describes persistent structural problems, so it is not a clean success narrative.

evidence.title: Pobreza infantil y adolescente en México-2022
evidence.claim: UNICEF found that children and adolescents remained the group with the highest poverty rates; indigenous children had extreme poverty of 50.2 percent and 93.9 percent lacked social security, while the first childhood cohort had poverty of 48.1 percent and the report says social-protection programs helped reduce poverty and should be universal and complemented by quality services.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent UN analysis with explicit quantitative findings on vulnerable groups and policy implications.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to federal policy because the report links reductions to social-protection programs, but it also reflects inherited inequality and structural gaps.
contrary_evidence: The same findings show large remaining deprivation and unequal access, especially for indigenous and early-childhood groups.

evidence.title: Pensión para el Bienestar de las Personas con Discapacidad Permanente
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Bienestar / Gobierno de México
evidence.claim: The 2022 disability-pension program page describes a rights-based objective to improve income for people with permanent disability and explicitly links the program to reducing discrimination, racism, and marginalization affecting children, youth, indigenous people, and Afro-Mexicans with disabilities.

AMLO was still Mexico’s president in 2022. The legal frame is strong on paper but constrained in practice: the presidency holds the federal executive power, is single-person, six-year, and non-reelectable, yet it is checked by Congress, the courts, the electoral authorities, autonomous bodies, and a fragmented security environment. I did not use the client matrix, and I did not re-fetch the structured local-prior facts you already supplied.

**Office, authority, constraints**
- Office: president of Mexico, the single head of the federal executive.
- Authority: executive appointment/removal, regulations, foreign policy execution, agenda-setting, and substantial agenda control through the daily briefing system and presidency-centered communication.
- Constraints: no re-election, supermajority requirements for constitutional change, Congress’s ability to block reforms, Supreme Court review, autonomous electoral and oversight bodies, and a violent/security environment that limits governability.

**Major 2022 events**
- 10 Apr: recall referendum ratified AMLO politically but had no binding legal force.
- 7 Apr to 18 Apr: electricity-law victory at the Court, then constitutional-overhaul defeat in Congress.
- Apr onward: litio became the fallback policy banner after the energy setback.
- Feb to Sep: continuing conflict with media, attacks on journalists, and public stigmatization of critics.
- Aug to Sep: AMLO moved toward keeping the military in public-security roles beyond 2024.
- 30 Sep: military data hack exposed state vulnerability and details about his health.

**Inherited conditions**
- Entrenched organized violence and journalist killings.
- Weak rule of law and low trust in institutions.
- A divided legislature after the 2021 midterms.
- Legal and market conflict over energy policy inherited from the 2013 reform era.
- Severe pressure on media freedom and a polarized information environment.

- `Q1 2022`: press hostility, journalist killings, media conflict.
- `Q2 2022`: recall referendum, energy-law and electricity-reform battles, litio pivot.
- `Q3 2022`: military/security expansion, fourth government report, governance stress.
- `Q4 2022`: cyber-hack exposure, continued centralization of security and communication.

**Gap Status**
- Appointments and delegation: partly resolved. The fiscal and spending core now has explicit 2022 appointment evidence, but I still do not have a complete cabinet-wide delegation map.
- Program-to-implementation: partly resolved. IMSS-Bienestar and the health-program decree show real operationalization, not just slogans.
- Regulatory predictability and anti-capture: partly resolved in the negative direction. The current record still supports uncertainty around energy and investment rules, but I did not find a cleaner 2022 sectoral implementation audit in this round.
- Outcome attribution: partly resolved. The 2022 poverty improvement is better grounded now, but the exact AMLO share is not recoverable from current evidence because labor-market conditions and remittances materially contributed.
- Exact causal decomposition: not recoverable in this round.

**Search and Rejection Summary**
- I checked about a dozen additional documents in this follow-up, mainly SHCP, Senate, IMSS, DOF, World Bank, OECD, IMF, and CONEVAL items.
- I kept only the sources that changed the gap picture: executive appointments, health federalization, and external attribution for the 2022 poverty decline.
- I rejected duplicate mirrors of the same official statements, plus broader macro context that was already covered in the current index and did not add a new AMLO-specific implementation link.
- I did not find a better direct audit of the full 2022 delegation chain or a more precise decomposition of the 2022 poverty decline than the sources already cited here.
